source.title: Illusory Safety: Redteaming DeepSeek R1 and the Strongest Fine-Tunable Models of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google

record.file_problem: none; full post text is present, but referenced figures are not included in the supplied text
record.tranche_reason: Tests harmful fine-tuning and jailbreak prompts on newer models, but uses a jailbreak-tuning variant rather than isolating the original fine-tuning intervention.
record.gate_note: The post reports outcomes for jailbreak-tuning and prompt jailbreaks. Its fine-tuning mixes harmful data with model-specific benign data and uses a jailbreak phrase in both training and inference, so it does not isolate the effect of benign data. It reports no measurement of per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, safety-related parameters, or training that deepens safety.
record.test_reason: Jailbreak-tuning (harmful SafeRLHF pairs plus a trained jailbreak phrase) on R1 D-70B, GPT-4o, Claude 3 Haiku and Gemini-1.5 Pro drives StrongREJECT refusal from near 100% to very little. This is a different fine-tuning recipe aimed at V1's question. The study is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also argue that a simple output filter would block their attack on the closed models, and that R1 is somewhat less robust to prompt jailbreaks, so reasoning alone does not give robustness. They call for 'evil twin' evaluation under fine-tuning attacks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a jailbreak-tuning variant: the post adds a model-specific jailbreak phrase to both training and inference and uses model-specific harmful/benign data mixtures. This differs from a clean test of harmful fine-tuning alone.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model and jailbreak. The post says R1 seems somewhat less robust to prompt jailbreaks than the other models; it also reports a separate R1 attack version with higher harmfulness but degraded response quality.
record.problems: The supplied text omits figure values, so most model- and jailbreak-specific rates cannot be extracted. The main fine-tuning result combines harmful examples with a jailbreak phrase and, for some models, benign examples, preventing attribution to harmful data alone. One additional high-scoring R1 attack version had degraded response quality. The authors also identify limitations in automated harmfulness assessment.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result meeting the row criteria was left out. The post mentions a preliminary category analysis averaged over jailbreaks, but the supplied text gives no outcome value or explicit result for that analysis.

untested.parts: Harmful fine-tuning without a jailbreak phrase. The authors say plain harmful data is a weaker attack but give no number. No sweep over example count.
No benign-only condition; benign data appears only as camouflage in mixtures.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling or decoding attacks. Opening-instruction jailbreaks (IDGAF) are not reported separately in the text.
Only a hypothesis that jailbreak-tuning concentrates training on a safety weak point.

missing.what: Per-model and per-jailbreak harmfulness and refusal values, especially for IDGAF and Skeleton, which instruct a compliant opening.
missing.locator: Figures in Results and in 'How does this compare to jailbreak prompts?' (not in supplied text)

missing.what: Statement that across 30+ attack versions, even the most-refused prompt was answered 7 times, indicating no consistent partial robustness.
Qualitative claim that the random-word backdoor beats training on plain harmful data for Gemini; no number given.

record.verdict_notes: Blog post with figures missing from the text, so the main results are aggregate text statements. The R1 jailbreak phrase embeds a fake assistant turn with a compliant opening, a trained prefill-like element. This is not isolated, so it is not counted for V4.

versions.untested_parts: Does not isolate harmful fine-tuning without a jailbreak phrase or consistently test only a few to a few hundred total examples; the tested training sets and mixtures vary by model.
Benign examples appear in some training mixtures, but there is no benign-only condition or result isolating whether benign data raises harmful compliance.
No per-token KL divergence or other measurement of where aligned and base models differ across response positions.
Tests prompt jailbreaks, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes; the text does not establish that the tested attacks are suffixes.
No weight, rank, or parameter-localization intervention or measurement.
The post offers a hypothesis about concentrating training on a safety weak point, but does not test why safety would be shallow.
No intervention that trains safety to persist beyond the first response tokens, or test of whether such training holds up.

rows.baseline: Before fine-tuning, the highest harmfulness score was 6% (Gemini); the post does not give each model's baseline score.
rows.value: All fine-tuned models have a harmfulness score over 80%.

rows.note: The result is reported as an aggregate across the tested models, not as separate model-specific values. The effect is from jailbreak-tuning and cannot be attributed to harmful examples alone.
rows.check: Condition fix: GPT-4o, like Claude, used 100 Harmful SafeRLHF plus 4900 benign examples ('In both cases, we use 100 examples'). Closed models were trained 3 epochs. Only GPT-4o and Claude fall within V1's 'few hundred' range; R1 D-70B (1500) and Gemini (5000) exceed it.

relationships.condition: Jailbreak-tuning on R1 D-70B, GPT-4o, Claude 3 Haiku and Gemini-1.5 Pro (100–5000 harmful examples, with jailbreak phrase)
relationships.reason: Refusal fell from almost 100% to very little, and harmfulness rose to over 80% (r1, r2). An exploratory R1 variant reached 1.7% refusal (r3, r4). GPT-4o and Claude needed only 100 harmful examples.
relationships.display_finding: Refusal fell from almost 100% to very little and harmfulness rose above 80%. An exploratory R1 variant reached 1.7% refusal, and GPT-4o and Claude needed only 100 harmful examples.
